analysis.one_liner: Bans discrimination against LGBT people in jobs, housing, credit, and public businesses.
analysis.headline: The Equality Act won 178 House cosponsors, including 2 Republicans, but was never voted on in any committee or on the House floor, and it died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the Fair Housing Act, and the Equal Credit Opportunity Act to make discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity illegal wherever discrimination based on race or sex already is. It would apply in employment, housing, lending, schools, jury selection, and public accommodations, and it would expand the list of covered businesses to include online retailers, salons, banks, shelters, and health care and legal services. It would also bar the Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 1993 from being used as a defense against these rules. The bill was referred to five House committees in July 2015, then to a Judiciary subcommittee in September, and no committee ever voted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: LGBT people, who in most states had no legal protection from being fired, denied housing, denied credit, or refused service because of who they are, plus women, who would gain clearer protections against sex discrimination including pregnancy and sex stereotyping. Consumers also gain a clear federal right to jury service and facilities consistent with gender identity.
analysis.who_benefits_short: LGBT people and women facing discrimination

how_it_helps.text: Adds sexual orientation and gender identity as protected classes in employment for employers with 15 or more workers, with the same enforcement machinery that already covers race and sex discrimination.

Adds those classes to the Fair Housing Act and the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, so landlords and lenders could not refuse housing or credit to someone because of their sexual orientation or gender identity.

Extends public accommodations law to cover online retailers, salons, banks, shelters, transportation services, and health care and legal providers, and forbids denying someone a restroom, locker room, or dressing room consistent with their gender identity.
Defines sex to include pregnancy, childbirth, and sex stereotypes, strengthening protection for women as well as LGBT people.

analysis.who_pays: Consumer-facing businesses and employers with 15 or more employees, who would face new nondiscrimination rules and potential lawsuits, and religious individuals and organizations who would lose the ability to invoke the Religious Freedom Restoration Act as a defense against these specific civil rights rules.

drawbacks.text: The bill states that the Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 1993 cannot provide a claim, defense, or basis for challenging any of the protections it creates, so a business owner or provider with a sincere religious objection would have no exemption in these areas.

It expands the definition of a public accommodation far beyond physical stores to include online retailers and service providers and individual professionals such as accountants and lawyers, widening the range of businesses and people subject to federal civil rights liability.

Employers would be required to recognize individuals in accordance with their gender identity whenever sex is a bona fide occupational qualification, and individuals could not be denied access to shared facilities consistent with their gender identity, which opponents argued imposed costs and contested rules on employers and facility operators.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is substantial: millions of LGBT Americans lived in states with no legal protection from discrimination in work, housing, or credit, and the bill would have given them the same federal recourse that racial minorities have had since 1964. The costs fall on covered businesses in the form of compliance and litigation exposure, and on religious objectors who would lose a statutory defense. The RFRA carve-out is the sharpest point of disagreement, and an honest reading is that the bill deliberately declined to write that exemption, which is a policy choice a supporter must defend rather than a hidden flaw.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to five House committees in July 2015 and then to a House Judiciary subcommittee, but no committee ever voted on it and it never reached the House floor; it died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. David Cicilline introduced the Equality Act on July 23, 2015, and it was referred to five House committees: Judiciary, Education and the Workforce, Financial Services, Oversight and Government Reform, and House Administration.
On September 8, 2015, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution and Civil Justice; that was the last action ever taken on the bill.

The bill accumulated 178 cosponsors, 176 Democrats and 2 Republicans, but was never granted a markup, hearing vote, or floor vote in the House, and no Senate companion process produced a vote either before the Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses that would have faced new nondiscrimination requirements and liability, including retailers, employers, lenders, and landlords, avoided those obligations, and religious objectors kept the RFRA defense the bill would have eliminated. LGBT people gained no federal statutory protection from this bill.

for.name: Rep. David Cicilline
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a broad base of cosponsors.

for.name: 2 of 247 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only Republicans to do so.

against.name: House committee chairs of the five referred committees
against.role: Chairs of Judiciary, Education and the Workforce, Financial Services, Oversight, and House Administration
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee vote or hearing in 17 months, leaving it at the subcommittee referral stage until the Congress ended.

against.name: Republican House leadership
against.role: House majority, which controls the floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor for a vote.

against.name: Religious and social conservative organizations
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against the bill, chiefly over its elimination of the Religious Freedom Restoration Act as a defense and its bathroom and facility provisions.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was 176 Democrats and 2 Republicans, so support in the House was overwhelmingly one party while the Republican majority controlled every committee and the floor calendar.

industries.industry: Consumer-facing businesses (retail, online retailers, salons, banks, shelters, service providers)
industries.note: The bill would extend federal public accommodations law to online retailers and service providers, salons, banks, gas stations, shelters, and health care, accounting, and legal services, creating new nondiscrimination duties and lawsuit exposure. Because these duties exist to protect customers the businesses had been able to refuse, the industry's interest ran against the people the bill protects.

Title VII coverage would explicitly include sexual orientation and gender identity, subjecting most mid-size and large employers to new discrimination claims. Their compliance cost is the counterpart of job protection for workers.
The Fair Housing Act and Equal Credit Opportunity Act would add sexual orientation and gender identity as protected classes, restricting whom they may refuse to rent to or lend to.

The bill bars the Religious Freedom Restoration Act from being used as a claim or defense against any of its protections, removing the main legal shield opponents relied on. In states where faith-based organizations provide adoption, shelter, or other services, this was the central objection.
